nodes.title: A locus for a human hereditary cataract is closely linked to the gamma-crystallin gene family.

nodes.label: Lubsen et al. (1987) studied a family in which a hereditary Coppock-like cataract of the embryonic lens nucleus occurred in heterozygotes, using Taq I RFLPs within the gamma-crystallin gene cluster. A haplotype (P), not seen among the haplotypes found in the Dutch and English population, was present only in family members with cataract, and all affected members carried it. This showed close linkage between the gamma-crystallin gene cluster and the cataract locus, with a maximum lod score of 7.58 at theta = 0.

Lubsen et al. (1987) concluded that the linkage of the Coppock-like cataract to the gamma-crystallin gene cluster provided genetic evidence that the primary cause of a cataract in humans could possibly be a lesion in a crystallin gene.

Brakenhoff et al. (1994) found that the locus for hereditary Coppock-like cataract (CCL) was closely linked to a particular combination of polymorphic TaqI sites within the human gamma-crystallin gene cluster. Mapping of these sites defined a 15-kb region that includes the gamma-D and psi-gamma-E genes.

Brakenhoff et al. (1994) cloned the gamma-D and psi-gamma-E genes from the Coppock-like cataract chromosome. The gamma-D gene worked the same as its allele cloned from a wild-type chromosome. The psi-gamma-E pseudogene from the CCL chromosome had a cluster of sequence changes within and around its TATA box. Together, these changes increased psi-gamma-E promoter activity tenfold, raising its expression to 30% of that of the gamma-D gene.

nodes.label: Brakenhoff et al. (1994) predicted that the protein encoded by the psi-gamma-E gene is a 6-kD N-terminal gamma-crystallin fragment. They suggested that reactivation of the psi-gamma-E gene, with resulting overexpression of this fragment, could cause Coppock-like cataract.

Scott et al. (1994) described a 7-generation family in which 48 of 138 individuals were known to have autosomal dominant congenital cataracts of the pulverulent type. Of 53 family members examined, 28 had congenital cataracts: 19 were unilateral (8 right eyes and 11 left eyes) and 9 were bilateral. The clinically unaffected eye in unilateral cases showed no lens opacity on detailed slit-lamp examination. Including historical data, there were 48 affected members (28 unilateral, 17 bilateral, and 3 obligate carriers who were not examined).

Scott et al. (1994) found that cataract severity varied within the family. Cases ranged from a subtle unilateral zonular cataract with 20/20 vision, to bilateral inner fetal nuclear pulverulent opacities with 20/16 vision in both eyes, to dense unilateral and bilateral nuclear cataracts that required early surgery. The authors reported that the autosomal dominant gene was expressed in an apparently random way as either unilateral or bilateral cataract. To their knowledge, this was the first such family described in the literature.
Héon et al. (1999) mapped aculeiform cataract to the gamma-crystallin (CRYG) locus on chromosome 2q33-q35.

In a family with aculeiform cataract, Héon et al. (1999) identified a mutation in exon 2 of the CRYGD gene by mutational analysis of the CRYG gene cluster. The mutation affected a highly conserved amino acid and was suggested to be associated with impaired folding of CRYGD; it was not seen in a large control population.

nodes.label: Héon et al. (1999) found that the previously reported Coppock-like cataract mutation in the pseudogene CRYGE was a polymorphism present in 23% of their control population. Further analysis of the original Coppock-like cataract family identified a missense mutation in a highly conserved segment of exon 2 of CRYGC, which was not found in a large control population; the authors considered this the first evidence of CRYGC involvement in human cataract.

nodes.label: Ren et al. (2000) studied a previously described 7-generation family in which 30 members had highly variable autosomal dominant zonular pulverulent cataracts.

Ren et al. (2000) mapped the cataracts in this 7-generation family to a 19-cM interval on chromosome 2q33-q35 that includes the gamma-crystallin gene cluster. The maximum lod scores were 4.56 (theta = 0.02) with D2S157, 3.66 (theta = 0.12) with D2S72, and 3.57 (theta = 0.052) with CRYG.

In the family with variable zonular pulverulent cataract, Ren et al. (2000) found a heterozygous 5-bp duplication in exon 2 of the gamma-C-crystallin gene (CRYGC). It was present in one allele of every affected family member and absent from both unaffected family members and unaffected controls. The mutation disrupts the reading frame and was predicted to produce an unstable gamma-C-crystallin made up of 38 amino acids of the first Greek key motif followed by 52 random amino acids. The CRYGD gene showed no abnormalities.

nodes.label: Ren et al. (2000) sequenced the pseudo-gamma-E-crystallin (CRYGEP) promoter region and used allele-specific oligonucleotide analysis in members of the pedigree. They concluded that activation of the gamma-E pseudogene was unlikely to cause the cataracts. Because base changes in the TATA box were also found in unaffected controls, these changes were excluded as a sole cause of cataract.
Ren et al. (2000) suggested that their finding shows mutant beta-gamma-crystallins do not need to associate appropriately into oligomers to cause cataracts.
Santhiya et al. (2002) reported novel mutations in the gamma-crystallin genes that cause autosomal dominant congenital cataracts.
Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) described a family with autosomal dominant primary congenital cataract of the nuclear type in which several members were affected.

In affected members of a family with autosomal dominant nuclear congenital cataract, Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) sequenced the CRYGA-D gene cluster and found a heterozygous c.502C>T transition in the CRYGC gene, causing an arg168-to-trp (R168W) substitution. The mutation segregated with the disease and was not found in healthy family members or in 170 unrelated controls. Although the variant was listed as a SNP in the NCBI database, the authors concluded that R168W is the actual disease-causing mutation.

Gonzalez-Huerta et al. (2007) noted that the CRYGC R168W mutation had previously been associated with lamellar cataract. They concluded that their family, which had nuclear cataract, was the first case of phenotypic heterogeneity specifically associated with this mutation.

Zhang et al. (2009) studied a 4-generation Chinese family from a relatively isolated region of northern China in which 6 members had autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea, with no other ocular or systemic abnormalities. Affected individuals had bilateral congenital nuclear cataracts, a central nuclear opacity involving the embryonic, fetal and infantile nucleus of the lens. They also had small eyeballs and corneas about 9 to 10 mm in diameter. Every affected individual had visual acuity of hand movements in front of the eye, together with nystagmus and amblyopia.

Zhang et al. (2009) reported that in the Chinese family autosomal dominant inheritance was supported by affected individuals in each of 4 generations and by male-to-male transmission. Penetrance appeared to be virtually complete.

Zhang et al. (2009) carried out a genomewide linkage scan in the Chinese family. The maximum 2-point lod score was 2.29 at marker D2S325 (theta = 0.0). Haplotype analysis placed the disease locus in a 19.04-cM region at 2q32.3-q35 between D2S117 and D2S2382. This region contains the gamma-crystallin gene cluster.

In the Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract and microcornea, Zhang et al. (2009) sequenced the candidate genes CRYGA through CRYGD. They found a heterozygous c.470G>A change in exon 3 of CRYGC, which converts the conserved tryptophan at codon 157 to a stop codon (W157X). The variant cosegregated with the disease and was absent from 100 normal controls. The authors predicted that it truncates the last 17 amino acids and disrupts the fourth Greek key motif.
Zhang et al. (2009) proposed that CRYGC mutations which disrupt lens biochemistry early in development may cause microphakia, with microcornea arising secondarily from damage to the lens.
Li et al. (2012) described a 3-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract.

In a 3-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract, Li et al. (2012) identified a heterozygous c.385G-T mutation in the CRYGC gene by candidate gene sequencing, resulting in a gly129-to-cys (G129C) substitution at a highly conserved residue. Molecular modeling and spectroscopic studies indicated that the mutation impaired the tertiary structure of the protein by modifying the H-bonding network in the C-terminal domain, and it dramatically decreased thermal stability and increased aggregation propensity under high concentration, heat, and UV irradiation stresses.
Li et al. (2012) showed that expression of the gamma-C-crystallin G129C mutant in zebrafish caused vacuoles and incomplete denucleation of the lens, recapitulating the human cataract phenotype.

Guo et al. (2012) described a 4-generation Chinese family in which 6 members had isolated bilateral autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataracts and microcornea. The nuclear opacities involved the embryonic, fetal, and infantile nuclei, and corneal diameter was about 9 mm in all affected members. All patients had nystagmus and amblyopia, and intraocular pressure was normal. The family had no history of related systemic abnormalities. The proband was diagnosed at age 8 years, and other affected members were diagnosed between 6 months and 13 years of age.

In a 4-generation Chinese family with autosomal dominant congenital nuclear cataract and microcornea, Guo et al. (2012) screened 9 candidate genes and identified a heterozygous c.471G>A transition in exon 3 of the CRYGC gene. The change converts a conserved tryptophan codon to a stop codon (TGG-to-TGA; W157X). The variant segregated with the disease and was absent from unaffected family members and from 100 ethnically matched controls. Bioinformatic modeling predicted that the variant truncates 18 C-terminal residues and partially removes the fourth Greek key motif. The authors noted that the same W157X protein change had been reported in another Chinese family with nuclear cataract and microcornea, where it arose from a different nucleotide change, c.470G>A (TGG-to-TAG).

Guo et al. (2012) noted that 2 families carrying the CRYGC W157X change, one caused by c.471G>A and the other by c.470G>A, both had nuclear cataract with microcornea. Other CRYGC mutations had been associated with Coppock-like, zonular pulverulent, lamellar, and nuclear cataracts. The authors concluded that W157X is disease-causing and should no longer be considered a polymorphism.

Guo et al. (2012) suggested that mutant CRYGC W157X transcripts may escape nonsense-mediated mRNA decay and be translated into a truncated protein that could have dominant-negative effects. Losing the fourth Greek key motif may disrupt the symmetric structure and folding of gamma-C-crystallin and change how it interacts with other crystallins.
